tagline.text: A Spanish colonial church on Lamon Bay that has outlasted pirates and earthquakes since the 17th century

location.label: Location
location.text: Manuel L. Quezon Street, Atimonan town proper, on the Lamon Bay coast, Quezon

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season; early August for the fiesta

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱600~1,500 (round-trip bus from Manila and meals, per person, day trip)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), then about 4–5 hours overland

children.text: Atimonan Church is the parish of Our Lady of the Angels on the Lamon Bay shore in Quezon. It was rebuilt several times after the Dutch attack of 1640 and took its present form around 1700. It is a National Historical Landmark, best seen together with Iskong Bantay, the pirate watchtower monument in front of it.

Atimonan Church, formally the Our Lady of the Angels Parish Church, is an active Catholic church under the Diocese of Lucena. It stands in the middle of Atimonan town in southeastern Quezon, where Luzon narrows toward the Pacific, facing Lamon Bay. According to Wikipedia, its coordinates are roughly 14.00°N, 121.92°E, about 172 km southeast of Manila and about 42 km from Lucena, the provincial capital.

The church's history reflects the turbulence of the Spanish colonial era. Wikipedia says the first church was destroyed by Dutch invaders in 1640 and that the present church was completed in 1700. Other accounts, such as Lumina, say the Dutch set the church on fire and it was rebuilt in stone instead of wood, was partly damaged by fire in 1648, and was demolished by an earthquake about two years later, and that a third church was restored between 1687 and 1701. Because the dates differ by source, the safe summary is that the church was destroyed and rebuilt several times in the 17th century and took its present form around 1700. It was badly damaged again by an earthquake in 1937, and in 1939 the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) declared it a National Historical Landmark.

In front of the church stands the Iskong Bantay monument. It is said to be the last surviving watch post built to defend the town against raids by pirates (Moros), and waypoints.ph says it stands about 130 m in front of the church and was built around 1752. The church and the watchtower face each other, so a single view shows both a place of worship and a place that guarded the town against threats from the sea, which is the main appeal of this site.

This is not a flashy tourist attraction. There are few official sources describing the architectural details inside and out, and a visit is mostly a quiet look around that fits between Mass and prayer times. It works well as a one-hour stop on the way to the Bicol region or the east coast, combining history with sea views, and during the early August parish fiesta you can see local devotion up close. Focus your photos on the exterior and the coastal scenery, and look around the interior quietly so you do not disturb worship. Rather than expecting a grand cathedral or a famous sight, think of it as a place to slowly read an old provincial church and watchtower, and you will likely enjoy it more.

blocks.title: A Spanish colonial church completed around 1700

children.text: Known to have been rebuilt after Dutch arson, fire and earthquakes and completed in 1700, this is still an active parish where Mass is held. It is both a historic site and a living place of worship.

blocks.title: National Historical Landmark and historical marker

children.text: The NHCP declared it a National Historical Landmark in 1939, and a historical marker stands on the site. Reading the marker gives you a quick sense of what the church has meant to the area.

Iskong Bantay, in front of the church, is introduced as the last surviving watch post built to guard against pirate raids. Seen together with the church, it helps you imagine how a coastal Spanish-era town defended itself.

blocks.title: A coastal setting facing Lamon Bay

children.text: The church faces Lamon Bay, so you get sea breezes and an open horizon along with the building. After your visit you can stroll along the shore and get a feel for the town.

blocks.title: The winged Our Lady of the Angels

children.text: Atimonan's image of Our Lady is known to have wings, standing on a globe and offering the Child Jesus. The devotion was brought by Franciscans in the 17th century and she is venerated as the town's patroness. She received an episcopal coronation on August 2, 2012.

blocks.title: The early August fiesta and the Karakol fluvial parade

children.text: The feast is on August 1–2. On the afternoon of August 2, the Karakol fluvial parade, begun in 1981, circles Lamon Bay led by a Grand Boat carrying the Virgin, then joins the land procession and ends at the church. It overlaps with the Tagultol Festival from July 29 to August 2.

blocks.title: A Visita Iglesia candidate in Quezon

children.text: It often appears in guides to Visita Iglesia routes of old Quezon churches during Holy Week. Eastern Quezon is too far to cover in one day from Manila, though, so it is more realistic to plan this church as its own stop.

items.title: Day trip
items.subtitle: The church and a walk through the coastal town

children.text: Take a bus from Manila (PITX, Cubao, Sampaloc and elsewhere) toward Lucena or direct to Atimonan. Terminals and timetables differ by operator, so check the day before.
Arrive in Atimonan town and head toward Manuel L. Quezon Street, where the church stands. Tell the driver "Atimonan Church" or "Our Lady of the Angels Parish" to avoid confusion.
Look around the church slowly, inside and out. If Mass is on, watch quietly from the back, and check the facade, the historical marker and the image of Our Lady of the Angels.
Walk to the Iskong Bantay monument in front of the church and check where the watchtower stands and which way it faces the sea.
Have lunch at a restaurant in town or on the shore. Seafood caught in Lamon Bay is a common menu item.
Stroll through a coastal park such as Atimonan Bay Park, or stop at a nearby beach.
Check the last bus to Manila and head back early.
The trip from Manila takes about 4–5 hours one way, so a day round trip just to see the church is tight. If you can, stay one night in Lucena or Atimonan.

items.title: Overnight trip
items.subtitle: Atimonan and its surroundings around the fiesta

children.text: Arrive in the morning, see the church and Iskong Bantay, and relax at a beach or the bay park in the afternoon.
In early August, watch the fiesta events and the Karakol fluvial parade. At other times, visit nearby waterfalls and caves such as Bantakay Falls.
Book accommodation and transport early during the festival.
According to Wikipedia, Atimonan is about 172 km from Manila. Go direct or transfer in Lucena.

A third-party route site lists A&B Liner from Sampaloc (Manila) to Atimonan at roughly ₱370–410 (2026, one site only), with departures at 3–5 AM and after 5 PM. We could not confirm this with another source, so check fares and timetables with the operator or locally.

Buses such as JAC Liner and DLTB run to Lucena Grand Terminal, with air-conditioned fares listed in 2026 at about ₱519 and a trip of about 3–5 hours. Fares appear to have risen recently, so check the latest price.
Rome2rio estimates about 5.5 hours and ₱850~1,100 from Manila to Atimonan including a transfer.
Bus operators and timetables change often. Ask the operator before you leave.

items.title: From Lucena by van or bus

children.text: Atimonan is about 42 km from Lucena. Vans from Lucena Grand Terminal are listed at roughly ₱150–250, running roughly from 7 AM to 7 PM (2026, one site only, so confirm the fare locally).
Buses such as A&B Liner also serve this stretch. Check the timetable locally.
From Manila, take SLEX and STAR Tollway into Quezon, pass Lucena and continue east. Depending on traffic it takes around 5 hours.
The church is in the town center, so parking nearby is limited. Check street parking rules locally.
Take a tricycle from the terminal to the church. The fare depends on distance and bargaining, so confirm before you ride.
The church and Iskong Bantay are within walking distance of each other.
You can visit the church all year. The eastern Quezon coast is in typhoon territory, though, so rain and wind in the wet season can make travel inconvenient.
To see cultural events, the best time is around the August 1–2 parish fiesta. The Karakol fluvial parade and the Tagultol Festival overlap then, but crowds and prices rise.

rows: Pleasant for the church and a town walk. The seas can be rough with the northeast monsoon

Atimonan town has small lodgings and beach resorts along the coast. Wikipedia mentions beach accommodations such as Villarreal Beach, ACEDRE Beach Resort and Playa De Lucia. Book early in peak season and during the fiesta. Facilities and prices change over time, so check the latest information.

Meals center on fish and seafood caught in Lamon Bay. You can try local food at the town market and restaurants, but business names and hours change often, so it is safest to ask locally. Because the trip from Manila is long, many visitors return to Lucena for dinner after seeing the church. Lucena is a large city with far more restaurants and lodgings to choose from.
The church is a place of worship. Dress modestly, covering shoulders and knees.
During Mass, avoid taking photos or making noise, and ask the parish office or the priest whether photography is allowed.
We could not confirm Mass times from official sources. Check the parish Facebook page or ask locally.
The church and Iskong Bantay are close, and seeing them together makes the history easier to grasp. Read the historical marker first.
A day round trip from Manila is tiring because of the long travel time. We recommend staying one night in Lucena first.
During the early August fiesta, lodging and transport get crowded, so book a month ahead and watch out for pickpockets.
The midday sun is strong, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
Bus fares and timetables change often, so check with the operator right before you leave.
The church is an active place of worship, so do not disturb Mass or rites, and recheck bus fares and timetables locally because they have changed recently.
The dates of construction and rebuilding in this guide differ by source, and are given as 1640, 1687–1701 and 1700. Trust the historical marker first.
In typhoon season (June–November), heavy rain and flooded roads can delay travel. Check the weather forecast.
Tricycles and vehicles are many during busy hours in town, so be careful crossing the street.
Keep valuables on your person and watch your belongings at crowded fiesta events.
We could not confirm the church's interior opening hours. Ask the parish before you visit.
